1boga7g:298: The core viewpoint of this article is that "credential leakage does not equal permission leakage" — this is a classic defense-in-depth idea applied in cloud-native scenarios. The security model of traditional AWS services is built on the assumption that abnormal usage of resources is accompanied by observable characteristics (such as abnormal instance types, CPU spikes). But Bedrock invocations do not have such "side effects" — an attacker's and a legitimate user's API requests are completely identical in form, which renders traditional anomaly detection mechanisms ineffective. The value of the AssumeRole layered model lies in decoupling identity authentication from business authorization. Initial credentials (AK/SK) can only perform AssumeRole, meaning that even if they are stolen, the attacker only gets a "semi-finished product" — they still need to pass the second gate of the trust policy (IP restrictions, time conditions, etc.) to obtain actual business permissions.

abpw0w:196: : SCP acts as a mandatory guardrail that cannot be bypassed by a member account's IAM Policy. The logical progression across these three layers is worth attention. IAM Policy is a "soft restriction" aimed at individual identities (it can be overridden by more permissive policies), while SCP is a "hard restriction" aimed at the entire organization (Deny takes precedence). In real attack scenarios, if an attacker obtains full administrator privileges by some means, IAM Policies may be modifiable, but the SCP Deny cannot be overridden—this is the essence of "defense in depth."
